text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, the elapsed time between the completions of A25 and A32 averaged about 0.87 hours (median about 0.89 h, middle half roughly 0.83–0.92 h) over 23 observed intervals; in the later window it averaged about 0.42 hours (median about 0.42 h, middle half roughly 0.39–0.46 h) over 30 intervals. The interval roughly halved, a drop of about 0.45 hours, and this difference is larger than in about 995 of 1,000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [TWAIT001]
- The elapsed time between the completions of A31 and A32 fell from about 0.10 hours on average (about 6 minutes, median about 0.06 h, with a wide middle half of roughly 0.03–0.18 h) over 26 intervals to about 0.04 hours (about 2.5 minutes, middle half roughly 0.02–0.06 h) over 27 intervals, with a noticeably tighter spread; this difference is also larger than in about 995 of 1,000 random re-splits. [TWAIT002]
- Both intervals end at A32 and were observed in only a modest share of traces (roughly 12–15 in 100 for A25→A32 and about 13 in 100 for A31→A32), so the two items plausibly describe one underlying timing behaviour rather than two independent differences. T_WAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completion events, not pure waiting or processing time. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence

The evidence is insufficient to infer a structural change in the process. Two items, both describing elapsed-time intervals into A32 and likely reflecting a single behaviour, are within the range an unchanged process typically produces (about 0.44 items expected by chance in this screening), and a shortening of elapsed time between completion events alone cannot establish a structural cause such as reordering, changed participation or changed routing. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Here we have 2 items when 0.44 is expected. Two items is the same order as the expectation (fewer than one expected, one or two items). So per the rule, this is what an unchanged process typically produces → Insufficient evidence.

The evidence contains no OCC/POS/REL/DIR items here — only TWAIT. So there's no relational or positional evidence. The instructions say a hypothesis about order or placement needs relational/positional evidence. Timing evidence alone supports... hmm, "Changes in participation, routing shares or repetition can support a hypothesis..." — timing isn't listed. So timing differences alone are weak for structural inference.

[TWAIT002]

Note: T_WAIT is elapsed time between consecutive completion events, not pure waiting or service time. Also both intervals end at A32, so they may reflect one underlying change around A32 rather than two independent differences. Support counts are modest (23–30 observations per window).
